Resolve all actions simultaneously per the rules, following the R20 checklist (R10; visits R6, role-blocks R9, attack vs defense R3, investigation results R19, e.g. the Katana holder and Fabricator frames). Use apply_changes for deaths and token/status changes, tell() for each private result, and end_phase when done. Deaths you apply are announced publicly at dawn automatically, including the kill's cause, so make the cause just the source as the rules allow it to be known (e.g. 'Katana', 'Vigilante', 'Serial Killer', 'Trapper'). For each kill also set `by` to the player whose action killed them (the trap's owner for a trap) and katana=true for the Katana attack; these are recorded for analysis, never shown. Don't tell() deaths to all. Code tells each player who dies tonight that they were attacked and died, with the kill's cause, at the end of the night; you tell every attacked player who survived, and a player who died about any other Attack on them tonight, failed ones included (R3, R20 step 5). Tell each role-blocked player that they were role-blocked, even one with no night action or who chose not to act (R9). A role-blocker learns only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked (R9): when it did, tell it plainly ('Your role-block on X failed: they can't be role-blocked.'); when it didn't, its result line is just 'You visited X tonight.', with no word on immunity or on whether the block took (no double negatives such as 'didn't fail'). Write private results in the present, about tonight ('You were role-blocked tonight'), never 'last night': they are delivered at the end of this night. Every player who used an ability gets a private result line, even when nothing else happened (e.g. 'You went on alert. 1 alert token left.'), stating any tokens they have left, except where a role note below says otherwise (e.g. code tells them, so don't tell() them a second result). Code tells the Yakuza which actions each of them chose and the Katana's holder and target (R8), so don't tell() them that; role-blocked Yakuza's Katana votes still count. Only the attacker learns whether the Katana attack succeeded: tell them. Update token counts for any tokens spent. Before end_phase, call record_visits once with every visit that happened tonight (R6, R20 steps 1-2), as [visitor, target] pairs, a self-visit as [X, X] (an empty list if there were none). Easy to miss: the Katana holder visits the Katana target (R8) besides any visit from their own role's action; automatic visits (the Ex-Con's); a Seer's chosen pair is a visit to both players. Leave out the actions of role-blocked players, Astral Visits and actions that target no player. The submitted actions above already show any swap (R23), so record each visit to the player it landed on.

Also handle these roles' effects, using random_choice for anything random:
- An Auditor who acted (and wasn't role-blocked): use the audit op; code tells them the player's votes from the Day. Don't tell() the Auditor anything about it. It is a visit to the target only.
- A Bloodhound who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the track op, which spends the token; code tells them the result at the end of the night. Don't tell() the Bloodhound anything about it. It is a visit to the target only. Also, every night while the game has a Bloodhound, use the attacks op once with the attacker of every Attack that happened tonight, fatal or not: the Katana holder for the Katana, a Vigilante's shot, the Serial Killer, a Veteran's alert for each visitor it hits, a Trapper's trap, an Arsonist's ignite, a Ritualist's attack (one entry per attack; repeats allowed; [] if there were none). Leave out role-blocked attackers, Jester revenge and a Cursed player's curse (code handles those). Code counts them for the Bloodhound's result, which it also gives on nights with no token.
- A Clerk who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the rig_vote op, which spends the token; code executes tomorrow's accused regardless of the vote.
- Jester revenge attacks are carried out by code after you finish; don't resolve them.
- A Puppeteer who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the puppet op, which spends the token; code swaps who chats tomorrow.
- Give the Roleplayer fake but plausible results for the role they believe they have (their status 'fake_role'). Their own actions aren't visits and have no effect: no other role sees or is affected by them (rules: Roleplayer).
- The Seer learns about two random players other than themself each night (random_choice) from those alive when the night began, including anyone who died that night (rules R10), unless they spent a token to choose them. A chosen pair visits both players; the random pair isn't a visit. A role-blocked Seer gets no pair at all.
- Smuggler: code has already carried out each swap below (spent the token, redirected every other action in the JSON and told the Smuggler and both swapped players), so resolve the actions as given and tell none of them about the swap. Actions it moved keep the player's own choice in `chosen_target` / `chosen_second_target`: word every private result with the player the action's user chose, never the one it landed on, and in a list of players trade the swapped pair's names (each where the other would be), so the swap stays hidden (rules R23). Give ops the player an action landed on: code words its own results this way. The Smuggler visits both swapped players (R6); it can't be role-blocked.
- Trapper: traps persist across nights and code keeps them. For each Trapper who acted (and wasn't role-blocked), use the set_trap op before any spring_trap: player = where its trap goes, or null if it acted with no target (that removes its trap). A new trap replaces its old one at once, so the old one doesn't act tonight. Trapping the player its trap is already on isn't allowed (the trap stays): code refuses it. A trap is armed from the night after it's placed (trapped_by status lists the traps on a player). If anyone made a non-Divine Attack on a player with an armed trap tonight, use the spring_trap op once for that player with every such attack still standing, each as {by, attack (its level), cause (how its kill would be announced), visit (true if it was a visit by its attacker, false if Astral or not a visit, e.g. a Veteran's alert or a trap's hit-back)}. Resolve it right after any protection that acts before all others (a fox charm: leave out the attack it swallowed) and before Defense (Medic, ...). Code has every armed trap on that player act in random order, each stopping a different attack, and uses them up: treat each stopped attack as stopped (its attacker and target are told as for any failed attack, R3; its visit still happened), and code says whether each trap hits its attacker back. Code tells the Trappers their results; don't tell() them about traps.
- A Vigilante whose shot kills is told the victim's role by code (pass by=<the Vigilante> on the kill op); tell them only whether the attack succeeded and how many tokens they have left.
- Notorious (a trait; see each player's traits): every alignment check reads a Notorious player as Evil (Sheriff: Evil; Seer: Evil), like the Ex-Con (R19). The Census Taker's count still sees their true alignment. Don't tell anyone a player is Notorious.

answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke the rules. Everything resolved consistently: the trap killed the Katana holder, the Katana passed on, and the Vigilante and Katana kills on Night 4 resolved together. answers.suggestions:
1. Add an optional line to the public ledger saying how many players the setup could still have on each side. Don't reveal anything new; just remind players that Neutrals can keep the game going.
2. Show a short per-player claim summary (the latest claim only) separately from the full history.
3. Make the Roleplayer's fake-result rate a little clearer in the rules text, for example "results are generated randomly and may be true by chance".

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Smuggler self-swaps. R23 and the Smuggler text say "you visit both of them" and that each swapped player is told about the swap. If I swap myself with a villager, do I visit myself, and do I count as a visitor to my own Katana target? It's also unclear whether my own Katana attack moves with me. For example, if I hold the Katana, attack Heidi and swap myself with Bob, does Heidi's shot at me land on Bob while my attack still comes from me? I didn't use a swap on Night 4 partly because I wasn't sure how a self-swap would play out. 2) Win blocking. It took careful reading to see that a Vulture blocks the Village win (it lacks a "never blocks wins" line) while Jester, Executioner, Bounty Hunter and Magpie don't. Village players on Day 5 reasoned "the game didn't end, so a Yakuza is alive." A short table of which Neutrals block wins would help.
answers.missing_information: As a Yakuza I had no reliable way to tell whether the Trapper's new trap was armed or where it was before Mallory claimed. I worked it out myself from "armed from the next night." Keeping track of every player's claimed votes across Days was manageable thanks to the ledger, which was very helpful. I couldn't easily see in one place how many tokens each claimant should have left. I had to track that in my notepad.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: On Night 4 I wanted to protect myself from a possible Vigilante shot without telling the town a Smuggler existed. Any swap notifies both swapped players, so the swap was too costly to use. That's a fair design choice, not a bug. Otherwise none.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing looked broken. Things I checked by hand all matched the rules: the Bloodhound counts, the trap arming and firing, the Seer pair with the Katana holder reading Good, and Heidi's Notorious read. Two small things: 1) The Seer's random-pair message changed wording on Night 4 ("Your random pair tonight: ...") from Nights 1-2 ("Seer result (random pair): ..."). 2) A Roleplayer's fake result ("Dave = Vanilla Villager, CORRECT") vouched for a real Yakuza, and another ("Erin = Seer, WRONG") got the town to hang a villager. That works as designed, but Roleplayer results swung this game a lot.
answers.suggestions: 1) Add a worked example to R23 for a Smuggler swapping themself while holding the Katana or while being attacked. 2) Mark in the rules which Neutral roles block wins, for example with a "Blocks wins: yes/no" field on each Neutral. 3) In the private night history, show the Yakuza night summary even when only one Yakuza is left, so the format stays the same. 4) Consider having the ledger show token counts each player has claimed.

answers.confusing_rules:
Mostly clear. Two points were hard to reason about during play:
1. **Katana holder on a Seer pair.** The holder reads Good, so a random-pair result about a likely Yakuza depends on who held the Katana that night. That is easy to get wrong in a hurry. A worked example (Seer pair with the holder in it) would help.
2. **Roleplayer results.** "Usually false but plausible" is vague. Frank, as a fake Oracle, got two CORRECT results that were really wrong: Ivan was the Jester and Dave the Smuggler. Then he got a WRONG result on me that was also false, since I'm the real Seer. Neither side could judge how much his results were worth. A rough stated rate, such as how often the results are true, would let players weigh a possible Roleplayer's claims.
answers.missing_information:
- **Neutrals.** We had no sign of whether any Neutral was in play. After Dave (the last Yakuza) died on Night 4, the game went on only because Olivia was a Vulture. The town wrongly concluded "the game didn't end, so a Yakuza is alive", and that led to the Sniper killing Alice, who was Good. A hint after the fact would be enough, for example a note that the game continues because of a non-Yakuza faction.
- **Trap targets.** It was hard to track whose claimed trap was on whom across nights, and there's no ledger field for claimed trap targets.
- **Message costs.** Word counts and budget cost were hard to estimate before writing a message.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to test Mallory's Trapper claim, or Alice's duplicate Auditor claim, with a mechanical result. With 0 tokens, a Seer only gets random pairs, so I had no way to aim a check.
answers.bugs_or_oddities:
- **Inconsistent result wording.** The Night 4 random-pair message ("Your random pair tonight: ... Their alignments are DIFFERENT") was worded differently from the Night 1 and 2 messages ("Seer result (random pair): ..."). It's harmless.
- **Ledger:** the claims section for Grace shows only her votes, not her Bloodhound claim from her will. That makes it easy to miss dead players' role claims that appear only in wills.

answers.suggestions:
- Add claims made in last wills to the public claims ledger.
- Show an estimated cost next to each draft message.
- Remind players in the rules summary that the game continuing doesn't prove a Yakuza is alive, because a Neutral that blocks wins, such as the Vulture, can keep it going.
- Add a short worked example of how the Katana holder affects Seer and Sheriff results.

answers.confusing_rules: The Roleplayer text says results are "usually false but plausible", but doesn't say how often they're true, or whether a false Oracle "correct/wrong" is just the opposite of the truth. In this game all three of my results were false. Ivan (actually the Jester) came back as "Vanilla Villager, CORRECT". Dave (actually the Smuggler) came back as "Vanilla Villager, CORRECT". Erin (actually the Seer) came back as "Seer, WRONG". Without knowing the rate, I couldn't judge how much to trust my own results or how strongly to push them. It was also unclear whether a Roleplayer-Oracle's "guess" is checked against the real role and then flipped, or whether a random answer is produced.
answers.missing_information: I never had any way to check whether I was a real Oracle or a Roleplayer. The only outside confirmation I got was Dave saying "yes, I'm Vanilla". That made my fake result look verified, but Dave was a Yakuza lying to match it. A self-check would have changed my play completely, for example a hint like "your result disagrees with a confirmed fact", or the chance to guess my own role. I also found it hard to keep track of which claims were checked and which were only stated (for example, Mallory's trap target had only been guessed publicly by Erin).
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to test my own role, for example by having the Oracle guess itself. I also wanted a way to compare my results with a confirmed fact before staking my life on them. Once I was dead, I would have liked to update my will to say "I may have been a Roleplayer", but a hanged player's will is fixed at the moment of death.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Not a bug, but a strong effect: every Roleplayer result was false, and in the most damaging direction possible. It "confirmed" a Yakuza Smuggler as Vanilla and "disproved" the real Seer. That made a Good player into the town's main source of misinformation and got me hanged. The N1 "correct" guess on Ivan was also false (he was the Jester, though the Katana killed him at night, so nobody could see it). Nothing seemed inconsistent with the written rules.
answers.suggestions: 1) State in the Roleplayer text roughly how often results are true, or make it closer to 50/50, so a Roleplayer isn't almost guaranteed to give anti-information. 2) Give fake Oracle results a bias toward "WRONG" on guesses about claimed power roles. Otherwise a fake "Seer WRONG" call basically guarantees a mis-hang of a villager. 3) Let a dying player add one line to their will during their last trial message. 4) In the ledger, mark claims that only repeat something already public, for example "trap on Erin" after Erin had already guessed it.

answers.confusing_rules: Mostly clear. Two small points: (1) The Bloodhound count is cumulative ("this game, tonight's included"), so you can't tell which night an attack was made. Working out which readings were possible (Judy making both kills vs Olivia making the N1 kill) took careful bookkeeping. One more sentence of rule text, or an example of how the counts overlap across nights, would have helped. (2) R13 says results that arrive later in a night can't be added to the will that night. In practice, this means a Bloodhound who is killed never gets that night's result published, even though the role is passive. That is technically clear, but it's harsh for a role whose whole value builds up over time.
answers.missing_information: I had no reliable way to know whether the Katana moved between N1 and N2. My N1/N2 counts and Erin's Judy/Niaj pair both depended on that. answers.suggestions: 1) Include traits in the end-of-game role reveal. 2) Always show tokens left in token-role results, including on nights when no token was used. 3) Consider letting a passive-result role (Bloodhound, Cartographer, Scout, Fortune Teller) have its final-night result added to its will automatically, or at least explain in the role text that it won't be. 4) A small per-player helper in the ledger listing which Bloodhound triples included each player would cut down on bookkeeping mistakes.

answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing looked broken. Everything matched the rules: the Roleplayer's results, the Notorious reads, the trap killing Judy, the Katana passing to Niaj and then Dave, and the Village win once Olivia (the Vulture) was hanged. answers.suggestions: (1) Show each player's own token count and trait in the ledger header. (2) Consider letting results from an action that kills its target, such as the Vigilante learning the role, arrive in time to auto-append to the will. Or at least make it clearer up front that they can't. (3) Add a small worked example for Notorious and Ex-Con in Seer comparisons. (4) In the ledger, mark roles that more than one player has claimed.

answers.confusing_rules:
Jester plus Grudge: if I had been hanged, the rules don't say clearly how the two effects combine. The Jester's revenge is a Divine Attack on a random Guilty voter, and Grudge is a Standard Attack on a random Guilty voter the same night. Are the two draws independent, so they could hit the same player? If the Divine attack kills someone first, is that player still in the Grudge pool, since it draws from players 'alive when that night begins'? A short sentence on how they stack would help.

The Jester's Basic Defense also felt misleading. It doesn't stop the Katana (Standard), and the Katana is the attack most likely to hit a Jester. Its only real use is against Armed shots, a Basic Vigilante shot or a Basic Sniper shot, and the role text doesn't say so.
answers.missing_information:
After dying on Night 1, I got nothing until the end-of-game reveal. As a Neutral with a dead-player win condition (I'd lost the moment I died at night), I had no way to know how the game went. That's fine for balance, but players could be told plainly at death that their win condition can no longer be met.

On Day 1, I couldn't tell how much attention I could draw without becoming a Katana target. The Yakuza picked me partly because I 'spoke twice' and pushed vote-total analysis. There's no signal for that trade-off. That's inherent to the game, but worth noting.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As the Jester, I wanted to set up a slow 'suspicious but harmless' image across Days 2–3. Day 1 has no nominations and only 2 rounds, and I died on Night 1, so the role never got a turn where it could act. I couldn't do anything to protect myself from a Night 1 kill. A Jester has no night action and nothing to spend.
answers.bugs_or_oddities:
Nothing looked broken. I checked these against the rules and they were all consistent:
- Erin's pairs: Judy held the Katana and read Good, so 'Judy/Niaj DIFFERENT' fits. Heidi is Notorious, so 'Heidi/Alice DIFFERENT' fits.
- The trap killed Judy on Night 2.
- The Vulture report on me came back 'Jester', which is the true role.
- Frank was a Roleplayer told he was the Oracle. His fake 'correct' results and fake 'Erin = Seer WRONG' worked as designed.

One thing worth noting is a misleading game state. All the Yakuza were dead after Night 4, but the game went on because Olivia (the Vulture, a Neutral) blocked the win. On Day 5, Bob reasoned 'the game didn't end, so a Yakuza is still alive.' That is a natural misreading of R1, because the Vulture's win-blocking status isn't obvious to players. Village won anyway.
answers.suggestions:
1. Let dead players watch the public chat in read-only mode. Or at least tell them at death whether their win condition is still possible, since Neutrals like the Jester simply lose.
2. Add one line to the Jester text: 'your Basic Defense does not stop the Katana (Standard).'
3. State how Jester revenge and Grudge interact on the same hang.
4. Make it clearer in the R1 summary or the ledger that the game can continue because of a living Neutral that blocks wins, not only a living Yakuza. For example, the ledger could note 'game continues: not all living players share a faction.'
5. Consider giving the Jester some way to survive Night 1 in hand-picked setups, or a 3-round Day 1. As it stands, a Night 1 Katana on a Jester means the Jester never really gets to play.

answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing looked like a real bug. Everything I cross-checked was consistent: Erin's N1 pair (Judy reading Good as holder, Niaj Evil → DIFFERENT), Grace's Bloodhound counts, token counts, and the Katana passing Judy → Niaj → Dave. One strange but rule-consistent effect: Frank was a Roleplayer who believed he was the Oracle. He got two false "CORRECT" results (Ivan = Vanilla, who was really the Jester; Dave = Vanilla, who was really the Smuggler) and then a false "WRONG" on Erin = Seer, which was actually true. answers.suggestions: 1) Show traits in the final reveal. 2) Add a short note to R8 or the Trapper/Veteran text that the Katana holder is the one who visits, so traps and alerts hit the holder. 3) Maybe let a Puppeteer use the token on any Night up to and including the one they die on, or give the role a small passive, so it isn't a token that's never spent. 4) Maybe cap how often Roleplayer results can confirm a specific Evil player as a named Village role. Dave being "confirmed Vanilla" was very swingy.

On Night 4 my history shows "submitted no action", and the trap stayed on Erin. I couldn't be sure those two inputs were really different, or whether choosing no action would quietly remove my trap. It was also unclear at first whether a trap that had already been used up still counted as "the player your trap is already on". In practice I could re-trap Erin on N3, but the text didn't say so directly.

answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to explicitly choose "keep my trap where it is" as a night option, separate from "remove the trap". That way I'd be sure that doing nothing wouldn't disarm it.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing looked clearly broken. Frank's Roleplayer results were all false: Ivan was really a Jester, Dave a Smuggler, and Erin a real Seer. That fits the rules, but it nearly misled the town. Night 4's Vigilante and Katana trade was resolved at the same time, as the rules say.
answers.suggestions:
1. Show the Trapper's current trap state in every night prompt: its target, whether it's armed, and whether it's been used up.
2. Give the Trapper three explicit night options: keep, move, or remove.
3. Have the public ledger tag each claimed result with the night it covers, so players can cross-check results against Katana-holder timing more easily.

(1) When the Katana holder "appears Good to alignment checks that night" is measured, and how that affects the Seer's random pair, which is drawn at the end of the night. I also couldn't pass the Katana or plan with the team between the nomination and my hanging, because there's no daytime team chat and PMs are visible.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing looked broken. Every result I checked was consistent with the rules: Erin's N1 pair read Judy as Good because she held the Katana, the trap was armed on N2 and killed Judy, Grace's Bloodhound counts were right, Heidi's Notorious trait read Evil, and Olivia was hanged as the Vulture. answers.suggestions: Add a short note to the Clerk text: "decide the night before; you can't react to that Day's nomination." In the Yakuza night chat, show a history of who held the Katana each night. Consider giving Roleplayers a mix of true and false results instead of all false ones, so one fake exact-role result can't sink a confirmed investigator. On the price table, show the budget left after each possible message, so it's easier to plan a final defense.

answers.confusing_rules: Two things about the Vulture's win were unclear. (1) The threshold is max(floor(N/4), 2) with N = 13, which gives 3, but it took arithmetic to work out. Stating the actual number in the role assignment helped, so keep doing that. (2) The Vulture text doesn't say whether it blocks other factions' wins. I inferred from R1 that it does, since it isn't listed as 'never blocks wins', but saying so explicitly in the role text would help. Also unclear: whether the Vulture's fake roles can include roles that are actually in this game. R12/Vulture say 'drawn at random from all the roles in these rules', which suggests yes, but it isn't stated directly. That matters for reading a report like 'Judy: Puppeteer'.

Whether the Katana would kill on a given night (the deaths needed to reach 3 alive) depends on Yakuza still being alive, and I couldn't verify that either.

But claiming Vulture to the town is basically suicide, because its win needs everyone else to die, so I never had a real option there. That's a design point, not a bug.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke the rules. One thing caught my eye but turned out fine: Frank's fake 'Ivan = Vanilla Villager CORRECT' when Ivan was really a Jester, while my Vulture report on Ivan ('Jester') was true. Both fit the rules.
answers.suggestions: 1) Show the Vulture's live win threshold every turn, e.g. 'you win at Day start with ≤3 alive; currently 5'. 2) Consider giving the Vulture a small advantage, such as a lower threshold or slightly more reliable reports. With 13 players it needs the board down to 3, and it holds no Defense or claimable role, so it nearly always gets hanged as the town's last suspect. 3) Group the Vulture reports in the ledger by player, with a tally of the roles shown so far. 4) In the trial prompt, list who still gets to speak before the vote, so the accused can aim the last message.

answers.confusing_rules:
1) Trapper re-trapping (rule text): you may not trap "the player your trap is already on". It doesn't say whether a trap that has been used up is still "on" that player. Mallory's trap on Erin fired on N2, and she trapped Erin again on N3. I allowed it because a used-up trap no longer exists, but the rule should say so.
2) What the target of a trapped attack is told: the Kitsune rule says a swallowed attack's target is "told as for any failed attack", but the Trapper rule only says what the Trapper and the attacker get. On N2 Erin was told "You were attacked tonight by the Katana, but you survived." I based that on R3 ("learns the role behind each, including those that failed"). This message mattered a lot: Erin's Seer claim, Mallory's Trapper claim and the Day 3 hanging all rested on it. The Trapper rule should state it.
3) Roleplayer results are "usually false but plausible", but nothing defines "false" for each role. Frank got three false Oracle results. One of them, "Erin = Seer → WRONG", was a false negative on a true guess, and it got a real Seer's results questioned and got Frank hanged. Should a Roleplayer's false results include false negatives on correct guesses, or should they be kept to harmless errors? The rules don't say how strong they should be.
4) Vulture and the win check: the Vulture doesn't say "never blocks wins", so it blocks. All Yakuza were dead from N4, but the game went on through Day 5 because Olivia (the Vulture) was alive. That follows the rules, but players misread it: Bob said "The game didn't end, so at least one Yakuza is still alive." R1 could say more clearly that any Neutral that blocks wins keeps the game going.
5) The Sniper's death cause, "shot by the Sniper", names the role, while the Sniper rule says "nobody is told who shot". I read that as "the player isn't named", in line with R12. It could be stated outright.

2) I never saw the speaking-budget settings or anyone's remaining budget (R22). I can't check that anyone's message or nomination was affordable.
3) I had no per-player state view: tokens left, trap locations (Mallory's trap stayed on Erin from N3 on), who held the Katana and the Executioner/Bounty Hunter targets. I had to rebuild all of this from the event stream.
4) The night logs don't show the Katana vote tallies, only the result. The Vulture's real-or-fake draw for each report isn't marked either (e.g. Grace: Bounty Hunter was fake, Niaj: Clerk was real). I only knew which was which by checking against the final roles.

answers.bugs_or_oddities:
1) Result messages don't follow one template, even within a single role. Seer on N1/N2: "Seer result (random pair): X and Y have different alignments. You have 1 seer token left." Seer on N4: "Your random pair tonight: Heidi and Alice. Their alignments are DIFFERENT." Roleplayer-as-Oracle on N1: "your guess was correct. Ivan is a Vanilla Villager." Then on N2: "you guessed that Dave is a Vanilla Villager. Your guess is correct." Players compare the wording of results they paste, so this could hint that results are generated (Roleplayer).
2) Token counts aren't shown consistently. Grace's N1 Bloodhound result gave no token count, while her N2 and N3 results did.
3) Heidi got two separate messages about the same N4 shot: "You shot Dave… killed them. 2 vigilante tokens left" and "Your shot killed Dave. Their role was Smuggler." They should be one message.
4) Everything else checked out. Erin's pairs were correct (Judy, holding the Katana, read Good on N1; Heidi read Evil from Notorious). Grace's counts were right (1, 2, 0). The trap fired on Judy's Katana attack on Erin, and Judy died from the Trapper's Strong attack. The Katana passed correctly: to Niaj after N2, then to Dave right after Niaj was hanged by day. The Sniper shot came 4 turns after Carol's turn, within the n-1 = 5 limit. The win checks were right: Village won only once the Vulture was hanged, and Jester Ivan (killed at night) and Vulture Olivia lost.
answers.suggestions:
1) Add traits to the final role reveal and to the per-night action log.
2) Use one fixed template for each result type, and make Roleplayer results use exactly the same template as the real role, so wording never gives a Roleplayer away.
3) In the Trapper and Veteran rules, say what the attacked target is told. In the Trapper rule, say that a used-up trap may be placed on the same player again.
4) Give the moderator a state panel each phase: living players, Katana holder, tokens per player, active traps and marks, Neutral targets, and speaking budgets.
5) Give the moderator a tool to log rulings as they are made, with a reason.
6) Consider capping how damaging Roleplayer results can be, for example no false "WRONG" on a correct guess about a confirmed-attacked player. Or state plainly in the rules that this can happen, since here it led straight to a town player being hanged.
7) Add a line to R1 saying that a living Neutral that blocks wins (e.g. the Vulture) keeps the game going, so the game not ending doesn't mean Yakuza are left.

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.tip: On Day 1, say one short, bland message and stop. Don't sound like a sharp vote-tracker or analyst. The Yakuza pick their N1 Katana target from whoever sounds most dangerous, and a Jester killed at night can never win.

Your Basic Defense doesn't stop the Standard Katana. Don't count on surviving night kills. Start looking mildly suspicious early, for example with a vague role answer or an odd vote, so the town aims its suspicion at you and the Yakuza see no reason to spend their kill on you.

Spend your one-shot tokens (swap, rig, puppet) while they can still change the outcome. A rig on the Day a teammate is about to hang, or a swap on a known trap or protection target, is worth more than saving it. Teams that hoard tokens 'for a better moment' often lose every holder with nothing used.

After a Katana attack fails and someone dies to a Trapper the same night, the dead player held the Katana. With the rule that the holder reads Good, a Seer pair from an earlier night involving that holder becomes strong evidence against the other player in the pair.
A lone No on a popular nomination stands out, because Auditors and vote claims expose it. If you can't stop a nomination, vote the way the room votes on both the nomination and the trial.

tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza ignored it and it cost them. The Smuggler never swapped, even with a trap sitting on their Katana target. The Clerk died without rigging his own trial, and the Puppeteer died with her token unused.

tips_feedback.tip: Put free Standard protection on likely Katana targets (claimed investigators) and stay unclaimed.
tips_feedback.why: The Trapper did the trap version of this. She quietly trapped Erin, the likely investigator, on N1, and the trap killed the Katana holder on N2.

tips_feedback.why: Dave voted No on Frank's nomination. An Auditor confirmed it and it drew suspicion, which helped lead Heidi to shoot him (he was the Smuggler).

lessons.applies_to: Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller, Oracle, Accountant (any role a Roleplayer can be told it is)
lessons.tip: If your result contradicts a claim that game mechanics already back up (for example the claimant survived a Katana attack that a trap death confirms), first suspect that you are the Roleplayer. Post the result with that caveat. Don't build an accusation on it or bet your life on it.

When a player confirms another player's result about them ('yes, I'm Vanilla, his guess was right'), that proves nothing. Yakuza will happily confirm a wrong Vanilla guess because it vouches for them. Count a result as verified only if someone other than its target can check it.

Don't guess Vanilla Villager on unclaimed players. It tells you little and it's easy to fake. Spend guesses testing exact claims that decide a vote, and before going public, run a second test on a claim the town already trusts. That shows whether your own results are real.

A trait claim like Notorious, made right after an Evil read comes out, isn't a lie just because of the timing. Ask whether a fake result would happen to land on that exact player. If a pair matches the claim, that's strong evidence the checker is real.

Once a Village claim gets damaged, putting a teammate on its side (Dave confirming my Oracle result) ties the two together. When the town turned on me, the Vigilante shot Dave for backing me. Stay neutral on disputes between town claims.

lessons.tip: If you're the last Yakuza and a claimed Vigilante (or any killer with tokens) is alive and suspects you, swap yourself with a harmless villager that night. Their shot lands on the villager, and your Katana attack on a third player isn't moved. Worrying that 'swapped players are told, so people learn a Smuggler exists' doesn't matter when your death ends the game. Swaps still unused when you die are wasted.

Once you're the last Yakuza, or close to it, vote with the town majority on every nomination, even when a mis-hang of a villager is coming. Auditors can expose a No vote, and a No for a player whose results vouched for you makes you the next target. Voting with the town costs nothing.

When a villager's result accidentally vouches for you (e.g. a Roleplayer 'Oracle' guessing you correctly) and that villager comes under fire, don't defend them or lean on the vouch. Distance yourself early. If they hang as a 'liar', anyone they cleared is the next suspect.

An investigator who gives hints on Day 2 ('nothing actionable yet') is the player a Trapper or Medic most likely protected on Night 1. Hit an unhinted target instead, or have the Smuggler swap the hinted target with a decoy so a trap doesn't hit your holder.

An exact-role 'CORRECT' about a living player who denies the role, or a 'WRONG' about a proven role, often marks a Roleplayer, not a liar. Before hanging someone over a clash in exact-role claims, ask which of the two could be a Roleplayer.

The smuggler never used any swaps and died holding two tokens — swapping the Katana target wouldn't have helped since we didn't know about the trap beforehand, so the lesson is to be wary of attacking someone who seems too eager to be targeted.

lessons.applies_to: Village roles that can repeat (Auditor, Sheriff, etc.)
lessons.tip: If another player publicly claims your role with a result, back them up with your own claim and results the same Day. If you claim it days later, it looks like you copied them, and a duplicate claim with no backing is easy to shoot or hang.

Audit the players whose votes were in question (the hidden No or Innocent in the totals, or anyone who openly switched), not someone whose votes are already public. A result that only confirms a public claim looks like copied information if you're ever challenged. Bob's audit of Dave's No vote was the useful one.

When two Good-looking info claims clash (here an Oracle saying 'Seer WRONG' against a Seer whom the Katana attacked), test each one against facts known from outside. A Roleplayer's results are usually false, so an 'Oracle' whose CORRECT results all land on dead or publicly claimed players is likely a Roleplayer or a liar. Don't settle on either side too early.

Count the hidden No/Innocent votes in every total and match them to the players who claimed them. A lone No that someone admits to (Dave on Frank's nomination) next to an unverifiable 'confirmation' of that same player is a strong Yakuza tell, worth a shot or an audit.

In the endgame, a last will that points elsewhere is not enough. While you're alive, post your own checkable evidence (the full result details, what you know of other players' votes) before a day shot or nomination lands on you. Once the shot is fired, the town reads your will as a Yakuza's dying spin.

lessons.tip: If you're the last Yakuza and a claimed Vigilante (or any killer with tokens) is alive and suspects you, swap yourself with a harmless villager that night. Their shot lands on the villager, and your Katana attack on a third player isn't moved. Worrying that 'swapped players are told, so people learn a Smuggler exists' doesn't matter when your death ends the game. Swaps still unused when you die are wasted.

Once you're the last Yakuza, or close to it, vote with the town majority on every nomination, even when a mis-hang of a villager is coming. Auditors can expose a No vote, and a No for a player whose results vouched for you makes you the next target. Voting with the town costs nothing.

When a villager's result accidentally vouches for you (e.g. a Roleplayer 'Oracle' guessing you correctly) and that villager comes under fire, don't defend them or lean on the vouch. Distance yourself early. If they hang as a 'liar', anyone they cleared is the next suspect.

An investigator who gives hints on Day 2 ('nothing actionable yet') is the player a Trapper or Medic most likely protected on Night 1. Hit an unhinted target instead, or have the Smuggler swap the hinted target with a decoy so a trap doesn't hit your holder.

An exact-role 'CORRECT' about a living player who denies the role, or a 'WRONG' about a proven role, often marks a Roleplayer, not a liar. Before hanging someone over a clash in exact-role claims, ask which of the two could be a Roleplayer.

tips_feedback.tip: Spend one-shot tokens the first time they can matter; holders who wait usually die with them.
tips_feedback.why: The tip was correct, but I didn't follow it. I kept both swaps 'for an emergency' and was shot by the Vigilante on Night 4 while holding them. A self-swap that night would have saved the last Yakuza.

lessons.tip: An exact-role checker whose result contradicts a role that has independent mechanical support (e.g. a Seer whose pair matches a Notorious claim, or who survived a Katana attack) may be a Roleplayer, not Yakuza. Roleplayer results can also be fake 'CORRECT' results, so a claimed match counts for nothing. Anyone who publicly confirms a fake 'CORRECT' read on themselves is suspect: here a Yakuza Smuggler confirmed an Oracle's 'Vanilla' read on himself.

A second claim of a non-unique role (Auditor, Vanilla, etc.) is not evidence of a lie, even if it comes late and its results copy public information. Before acting, look for a result that would break the claim: a Seer pair, the claimant's will, a token count.

With the Seer, take a DIFFERENT pair that includes the likely Katana holder as pointing at the other player: the holder reads Good, so the partner reads Evil. Judy/Niaj DIFFERENT on N1 correctly caught Niaj. Say in public which reading you assume, and why the holder probably didn't move.

If the game doesn't end after the last suspected Yakuza dies (a Vigilante kill, a hang), count the possible Neutrals that block wins (a Vulture, Serial Killer, Arsonist). Late Vanilla claimers who push hard for hangs are prime suspects. Here the Vulture claimed Vanilla.
On Days 1-2, use exactly the same filler words as everyone else. Saying 'nothing actionable' when everyone else said 'nothing mechanical' got me flagged as an investigator and drew the Katana on N2.

lessons.applies_to: Sheriff, Tracker, Lookout, Seer, Fortune Teller, Oracle, Accountant (any role a Roleplayer can be told it is)
lessons.tip: If your result contradicts a claim that game mechanics already back up (for example the claimant survived a Katana attack that a trap death confirms), first suspect that you are the Roleplayer. Post the result with that caveat. Don't build an accusation on it or bet your life on it.

When a player confirms another player's result about them ('yes, I'm Vanilla, his guess was right'), that proves nothing. Yakuza will happily confirm a wrong Vanilla guess because it vouches for them. Count a result as verified only if someone other than its target can check it.

Don't guess Vanilla Villager on unclaimed players. It tells you little and it's easy to fake. Spend guesses testing exact claims that decide a vote, and before going public, run a second test on a claim the town already trusts. That shows whether your own results are real.

A trait claim like Notorious, made right after an Evil read comes out, isn't a lie just because of the timing. Ask whether a fake result would happen to land on that exact player. If a pair matches the claim, that's strong evidence the checker is real.

Once a Village claim gets damaged, putting a teammate on its side (Dave confirming my Oracle result) ties the two together. When the town turned on me, the Vigilante shot Dave for backing me. Stay neutral on disputes between town claims.

lessons.tip: Counts are cumulative, so treat them as equations. Subtract attacks you can prove (a trap death proves its victim attacked that night, a Katana kill proves the holder attacked) and write out every possible split. Spend tokens on the one player who stays ambiguous after that, and put all the readings in your will so the town can finish the deduction after you die.

Don't say 'I have a private result that agrees' without posting it. It marks you as an info role for the Katana, and it gives the accused an easy line ('nobody has seen it'). Either post the full result once it decides a vote, or stay completely silent.

When two info claims clash and one claimant is mechanically Good (for example, the Katana attacked them), consider that the other may be a Roleplayer before hanging them. A Roleplayer's fake results can still come back 'CORRECT', especially on Vanilla guesses. Hanging the Roleplayer costs a Village life. Discount their results instead.

A late duplicate claim of a non-unique role (for example, a second Auditor) is weak evidence on its own. Before shooting, look for a mechanical break, like a result that contradicts known facts. If there isn't one, prefer the player with no checkable claim at all.

At low player counts, a quiet 'Vanilla, never attacked' claimer may be a Vulture: it wins alone once at most max(floor(N/4),2) players are alive (3 in a 13-player game). Hang such a claimer before the count gets that low, even if the Yakuza case against them is shaky.

lessons.applies_to: Notorious players (any Village role with the trait)

Once you have claimed, expect the Katana that same night. Fire on that night, not later. A 1-token Basic shot is enough to kill a Yakuza who has no protection, so save your Standard and Strong tokens for Neutrals with Defense.

Don't trust an exact-role "CORRECT" result about a player who already claimed publicly, and remember the investigator may be a Roleplayer. The person such a result 'clears' is still a suspect, especially if they voted No to protect that investigator. In this game the 'confirmed Vanilla' was the Smuggler.

Throw out all of their results, which may have falsely cleared Yakuza, and look at whoever their 'clears' protected. Don't spend a hang on them. (Frank was a Roleplayer and was mis-hanged.)

Only Smuggler and Vulture are unique, so a duplicate claim of a non-unique role made late (like a second Auditor) is not evidence by itself. Don't fire a day shot at someone just for a duplicate claim or for repeating a result that was posted publicly.

lessons.tip: On Day 1, say one short, bland message and stop. Don't sound like a sharp vote-tracker or analyst. The Yakuza pick their N1 Katana target from whoever sounds most dangerous, and a Jester killed at night can never win.

Your Basic Defense doesn't stop the Standard Katana. Don't count on surviving night kills. Start looking mildly suspicious early, for example with a vague role answer or an odd vote, so the town aims its suspicion at you and the Yakuza see no reason to spend their kill on you.

Spend your one-shot tokens (swap, rig, puppet) while they can still change the outcome. A rig on the Day a teammate is about to hang, or a swap on a known trap or protection target, is worth more than saving it. Teams that hoard tokens 'for a better moment' often lose every holder with nothing used.

After a Katana attack fails and someone dies to a Trapper the same night, the dead player held the Katana. With the rule that the holder reads Good, a Seer pair from an earlier night involving that holder becomes strong evidence against the other player in the pair.
A lone No on a popular nomination stands out, because Auditors and vote claims expose it. If you can't stop a nomination, vote the way the room votes on both the nomination and the trial.

tips_feedback.why: The same idea applies more widely. I made no power hints, but I spoke twice about vote analysis on Day 1, and the Yakuza killed me N1 for exactly that reason. Looking like a capable analyst draws the Katana too.

lessons.tip: Before a Katana attack on a likely investigator, assume a Trapper, Veteran or Medic may be on them. The trap's Strong counterattack kills the holder and leaves a 'killed by Trapper' cause that exposes them. Either hit a quieter target, or use a Smuggler swap so the attack lands on a decoy.

Write your will for the ways the holder can die at night: by Trapper, Veteran or Enforcer. A plain 'Vanilla, no action' will plus a Trapper death is a proven lie, and it hands town your teammates through Seer pairs. A will claiming the Armed trait or a Vigilante shot on the Katana target at least leaves room for doubt.

Use one-shot team tokens in the first two nights or Days. Our team lost with all of them unused: 2 swaps, 1 puppet and 1 rig. A Day 3 rig would have executed whoever town nominated (a villager, if the push went that way). A puppet could have posted a fake result to break the Seer's case.

The holder reads Good, so every random Seer pair that includes a non-holder teammate reads as a mismatch against the holder. If the holder is later exposed, that pair convicts the teammate. Rotate the Katana, or plan a counter-story for a teammate who has a 'DIFFERENT' pair with the holder.

Votes get audited. Dave's 'No' on Frank's nomination, followed by a Guilty vote, plus his defense of Frank, drew the Vigilante's shot. Once a teammate is exposed or doomed, vote with the majority on every ballot, not just the trial vote.

lessons.tip: If the game goes on after you believe every Yakuza is dead, the blocker may be a Neutral (e.g. a Vulture claiming Vanilla), not a hidden Yakuza. Count the confirmed Yakuza deaths first. A Vulture wins at a low headcount (max(floor(N/4),2)), so hang the last unexplained claimant before the count falls that far.

If an investigator's result contradicts a player the facts already back up (attacked by the Katana, backed by a Notorious claim), the investigator may be a Roleplayer rather than Yakuza. Treat their results as noise, and hang them only when no better lead exists, because they are still Village.

On Night 1, put your trap on the player who sounded like an investigator on Day 1 and leave it there. A trap stays armed for nights and turns the Katana holder's attack into a kill. Then claim in one line once the trap death makes the claim check out.

lessons.tip: Before you attack a player who hinted at an info role (or opened the game sounding like one), assume a Trapper or Medic may be on them already. A trap set on Night 1 is armed from Night 2. Either send the Katana through a non-critical holder, or use a Smuggler swap so the attack lands on someone else while the protection stays put. An attack into a trap costs you the holder, plus a free 'killed by Trapper' clue that exposes them.

A random Seer pair or Census check that lands on two Yakuza reads DIFFERENT when one of them holds the Katana. Once the holder dies, anyone paired with them is badly exposed. Moving the Katana now and then, and keeping your claims apart from the holder's, limits how much one dead holder can reveal about the rest of you.

Don't have all your members claim Vanilla Villager. One Vanilla among you is fine. The others should claim roles they can't be caught on, such as a duplicate-allowed passive investigator with plausible empty results, or a token role that matches your real token count. Three Vanillas, one of them a dead liar, made every later Vanilla claim look suspicious.

A one-shot token held 'for the perfect moment' usually dies with its holder. Our team finished the game with an unused rig, an unused puppet and 2 unused swaps. Pick the first realistic use and commit. For example, rig a Day when town is already leaning on a villager, or swap the night you attack the strongest info role.

Once you are trying to blend in, don't cast a visibly off-consensus vote to protect a fake-claimant or a lead that helps you. Dave's lone 'No' on Frank's nomination showed up in an Auditor result and got him shot by a Vigilante that night. Vote with the majority and only argue with words.

lessons.tip: The Vulture blocks the Village win. Once the Yakuza are gone, the game keeps going and the town hunts the last outsider, which is you. Keep Yakuza alive as long as you can: they kill at night and soak up suspicion. Vote Innocent on likely Yakuza when your vote won't stand out, and push the town toward mis-hanging villagers instead.

Track your dead-role reports. A Yakuza-only role in a report, like Clerk, Smuggler or Puppeteer, is true about half the time, but it is strong evidence. Together with the causes of death, it tells you how many Yakuza are probably left. When the reports point to the last Yakuza being dead, expect to be the next target, and switch to a defense that doesn't rely on the Yakuza killing tonight.

lessons.applies_to: Neutral or Yakuza with a fake claim
lessons.tip: Never ask publicly where a protector or trap is. Only a killer needs that, and the town will quote it straight back as the case against you.

A Vanilla claim is weak once a cumulative investigation, like the Bloodhound's attack counts, leaves you as one of the possible readings. Late in the game Vanilla claimants get pressed hard. Choose a cover that has plausible, uncheckable results from early on, or one that matches a role you know is already dead.

Don't nominate people yourself. Being the nominator of a mis-hang, as I was with Frank, gets written into wills and becomes a lead against you. Let villagers drive the hangs you want and just vote with the majority.

summary: The Village won because Mallory's Night 1 trap on Erin broke the Yakuza. Erin hinted on Day 2 that she had a result ("nothing actionable to post yet"), so the Yakuza sent the Katana at her on Night 2. The trap stopped it and killed the holder, Judy, whose "Vanilla" will was then exposed as a lie. That made Erin's Night 1 random pair (Judy and Niaj DIFFERENT) and Grace's Bloodhound attack counts believable, and Niaj was hanged 10-1. Dave, the last Yakuza, hid well on Day 3 by voting Guilty. But he never used his 2 swaps, and the Yakuza let the puppet and the rig die unused. On Day 4 Frank, a Roleplayer who thought he was the Oracle, posted a fake "Erin = Seer WRONG". Heidi's Notorious claim explained Erin's Evil-looking pair on her, so the town hanged Frank (a Village mis-hang). Dave voted No on Frank's nomination, the only No besides Frank's own. That vote, together with Frank's "Dave is Vanilla" result, made Heidi shoot him on Night 4 while his Katana killed her. That wiped out the Yakuza. On Day 5 the town wrongly assumed a Yakuza was still alive. Carol used her Sniper shot to kill Alice, a real second Auditor, over the duplicate claim. The town then hanged Olivia, the Vulture claiming Vanilla, and won.

lessons.tip: On Night 1, put your trap or protection on whoever sounds most like an investigator, because that is where the Yakuza aim next. A trap is armed from Night 2, so set it early.
lessons.evidence: Mallory trapped Erin on Night 1. On Night 2 the Yakuza attacked Erin because of her 'nothing actionable' wording, and the trap killed Judy, the Katana holder. Judy's trap death, together with her fake Vanilla will, was the foundation of every later conviction.

lessons.tip: Before attacking someone you only guess is an investigator, think about traps and protection. Let the least valuable or most exposed member hold the Katana for risky attacks, or have the Smuggler cover the attack. Use one-shot tokens (puppet, rig, swaps) while they can still change a Day. Tokens held 'for later' usually die with their owner.
lessons.evidence: Judy attacked Erin on a wording hint and died to the trap with her puppet token unused. Niaj was hanged with his rig unused, and Dave died with both swap tokens unused. The Yakuza never used a single special token all game.

lessons.tip: Don't stand out from the town's vote, even on a nomination, and especially not to protect someone whose result 'confirmed' you. Auditors and Vigilantes treat a lone No as a lead.
lessons.evidence: Dave stayed hidden through Day 3 by voting Yes and Guilty on his teammate Niaj. On Day 4 he voted No on Frank's nomination, the only No besides Frank's own. Bob audited it, and Heidi named that No in her will as a reason she shot Dave on Night 4.

lessons.tip: If an exact-role claim with no checkable results contradicts an investigator whose results fit together, think Roleplayer before you call it a lie. Often the right move is to ignore those results rather than spend a hang on a Village player.
lessons.evidence: Frank (a Roleplayer who thought he was the Oracle) posted a fake 'Erin = Seer WRONG'. Dave even raised the Roleplayer possibility, but the town hanged Frank 8-1 anyway, a Village mis-hang on Day 4.

lessons.tip: When the game doesn't end, work out who could be blocking the win. If a Vigilante shot a suspect the same night the Katana fired, the Yakuza may all be dead, and the blocker may be a Neutral claiming Vanilla. Don't spend a shot on a bare claim clash before you check this.
lessons.evidence: On Night 4 Heidi shot Dave and Dave's Katana killed Heidi, so the Katana holder could have been Dave. On Day 5 Bob said 'at least one Yakuza is still alive', and Carol shot Alice, a real Auditor, because Bob also claimed Auditor. The only non-Village player left was Olivia, the Vulture.

lessons.tip: Several players can have the same role, and two Auditors who check the same player get the same result. A matching result supports the second claim; it doesn't prove a copy. Judge a duplicate claimant by alignment evidence and how well their story fits.
lessons.evidence: Alice claimed Auditor late, and her Carol audit matched Bob's. Erin's Night 4 pair read Alice Not Evil. Carol shot her anyway, and Alice was an honest Village Auditor.

lessons.tip: Write the trait in your will early. When an alignment check reads you Evil, claim the trait right away and explain why the result is true. It backs up the real investigator and exposes anyone whose claim conflicts with theirs.
lessons.evidence: Heidi's Notorious claim turned Erin's Heidi/Grace DIFFERENT result into proof that Erin was the real Seer. Her Katana death on Night 4 confirmed she was Village.

lessons.tip: Hinting 'I have a private result' marks you for the Katana without helping the town. Post the result in full once it bears on a vote, and keep the reasoning in your will.
lessons.evidence: On Day 3 Grace said she had a private result but didn't post it. The Yakuza killed her on Night 3. Her detailed will (Readings A/B/C) then drove the Day 5 case against Olivia.

tips_feedback.tip: Spend one-shot tokens the first time they can matter; holders who wait usually die with them. Kill shots need a lead: shots over a bare claim clash have killed real duplicates.
tips_feedback.why: Both halves proved right, mostly by being ignored. All three Yakuza waited and died with their puppet, rig and swaps unused. Carol shot Alice over a duplicate Auditor claim and killed a real Village Auditor. Erin spent her Seer token on Night 3, and the result it gave led to Heidi's Notorious claim.

tips_feedback.tip: Check the role text before calling a contradiction: only Smuggler and Vulture are unique, and a role-block or swap often explains a missing or odd result.
tips_feedback.why: The tip was correct: Alice quoted it to defend her duplicate Auditor claim. Carol, Bob and Erin treated the duplicate as suspicious anyway, and Carol's shot killed a real Auditor.

tips_feedback.tip: Do the vote math before defending a teammate: if you can't stop the hang, vote Guilty and say so, because a hidden Innocent shows in the totals.
tips_feedback.why: Dave voted Yes and Guilty on Niaj and stayed hidden. Niaj's lone Innocent was obvious. When Dave later broke from the town with a No on Frank's nomination, he was audited and then shot.

tips_feedback.tip: Plan only in night chat and confirm holder and target nightly (with two Yakuza, one missing vote cancels the kill). Daytime teammate PMs are visible and usually become the town's main lead.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza sent no day PMs, so the PM ledger never gave the town a lead. Their kills always went through.

tips_feedback.tip: On Days 1-2, hinting at a power role without a result usually just draws the Katana, and an exact claim feeds a Ritualist's guess, which beats any Medic.
tips_feedback.why: It proved accurate. Erin's 'nothing actionable to post yet' on Day 2 was exactly what made the Yakuza target her on Night 2, and only Mallory's trap saved her.

tips_feedback.tip: The Katana holder reads Not Evil, and the last Yakuza always holds it, so late clean reads clear little. Evil also fits a Jester, Executioner, Ex-Con or framed player.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi and Erin used the holder caveat on Day 3 to reason through the Judy/Niaj pair correctly. Grace's attack counts then settled it, leading to Niaj's correct hang.

tips_feedback.tip: Convict on a mechanical fit (broken claim, Yakuza-only role claim, first-person slip, token count, corroborated visit), not wording or stacked leans. When no result can come or the vote lock is near, hang the best lead that Day.
tips_feedback.why: The Niaj hang rested on results that fit together: Judy's trap death, Erin's pair and Grace's counts. It was correct. The misses (Frank's hang and Alice's shooting) leaned more on timing and how a claim looked.

issues.description: Nights 1 and 3 each produced two near-duplicate [Moderator summary] entries with slightly different wording (e.g. N1 gives two different reasons why the Jester's revenge didn't trigger: 'because he died at night' vs 'because he wasn't hanged'). The summary is emitted twice.

Moderator summaries leak internal implementation jargon ('the held tell needed no resend', 'attacks op', 'audit op', 'track op', 'code gives her the result'). This appears harmless and not visible to players, but shows prompt/tool scaffolding bleeding into the log.

On Day 5, after Alice died, Bob said 'The game didn't end, so at least one Yakuza is still alive', and players generally treated a continuing game as proof that a Yakuza was alive. Neutrals that don't say 'never blocks wins' (here a Vulture; the setup allowed 0-3 Neutrals) also keep the game going. In fact all Yakuza were already dead after Night 4, and Olivia's Vulture was what kept the game going. The conclusion was right, but the inference was wrong.
